Part 1 · Fundamentals

How can a stream of air cool water below the air's own temperature?

Part 1 · the plan

Four ideas behind every cooling tower

  1. Two routes for the heatsensible heat to the air, latent heat carried off by evaporation
  2. Moist air in five numbersdry bulb, wet bulb, humidity, relative humidity, enthalpy
  3. Merkel's driving forcewhy enthalpy, not temperature, sets the fill a tower needs
  4. Range, approach and the water balancethe numbers an operator reads every shift

Why a tower works

Heat leaves the water by two routes

Sensible heat

Warm water heats the air; stops at the air temperature.

Latent heat

Evaporating water carries off ≈ 2 400 kJ/kg; works while the air is unsaturated.

Evaporation lets the water leave below the dry bulb; its limit is the wet bulb.

Moist air

Five numbers describe the airstep 1 of 2

Latent cooling depends on how much more water the air can take. That needs the air described.

$T_{db}$
dry bulb: ordinary thermometer (TI-230)
°C
$T_{wb}$
wet bulb: wet-wick thermometer, coldest evaporation reaches (TI-231)
°C
$w$
humidity ratio: vapour per kg dry air
kg/kg da
$p_s$
saturation vapour pressure of water
kPa
$\varphi$
relative humidity: vapour pressure ÷ $p_s(T_{db})$
–
$h$
enthalpy of moist air per kg dry air
kJ/kg da

Moist air

Three equations the simulator usesstep 2 of 2

$$\begin{aligned} p_s&=0.61078\,\exp\!\left(\frac{17.27\,T}{T+237.3}\right)\\[2pt] w_s&=0.622\,\frac{p_s}{P-p_s}\\[2pt] h&=1.006\,T+w\,(2501+1.86\,T)\end{aligned}$$

$P$ = 101.325 kPa (sea level). First line: Tetens' fit to the steam tables; $w_s$ = humidity of saturated air.

1.006 = $c_p$ of dry air · 2501 = latent heat at 0 °C · 1.86 = $c_p$ of vapour (kJ/kg·K).

Saturated air at water temperature $T$ has enthalpy $h_s(T)$ — the curve the next slides lean on.

Interactive — set the weather

What the wet bulb tells you about the air

humidity $w$ relative humidity $\varphi$ enthalpy $h$ of the air $h_s$ at the wet bulb

The air's enthalpy almost equals $h_s(T_{wb})$: the wet bulb, not the dry bulb, fixes what the air can absorb.

Merkel's driving force

A slice of fill: what we trackstep 1 of 4

The air's capacity is an enthalpy. So the transfer should be written in enthalpy too.

$L$
water mass flow through the cell
kg/s
$G$
dry-air mass flow drawn by the fan
kg/s
$T$
water temperature at the slice
°C
$h_a$
enthalpy of the air at the slice
kJ/kg da
$h_s$
enthalpy of saturated air at $T$ (film at the water surface)
kJ/kg da
$KaV$
transfer coefficient × area per volume × fill volume
kg/s

Merkel's driving force

Three ways to write the same heatstep 2 of 4

$dQ = L\,c_p\,dT$water cools by $dT$ across the slice
$dQ = G\,dh_a$all that heat ends up in the air
$dQ = K\,a\,(h_s-h_a)\,dV$transfer driven by the enthalpy difference

$c_p$ = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K), specific heat of water. $dQ$ in kW.

Third line is Merkel's step: Lewis number ≈ 1 lets heat and mass transfer merge.

Merkel's driving force

From one slice to the whole fillstep 3 of 4

From step 2 · water side and transfer$dQ=L\,c_p\,dT \qquad dQ=K\,a\,(h_s-h_a)\,dV$
$L\,c_p\,dT = K\,a\,(h_s-h_a)\,dV$both equal the same $dQ$
$\dfrac{K\,a\,dV}{L}=\dfrac{c_p\,dT}{h_s-h_a}$separate fill terms from water terms
$$\frac{KaV}{L}=\int_{T_2}^{T_1}\frac{c_p\,dT}{h_s(T)-h_a}$$

$T_1$ hot water in, $T_2$ cold water out. Neglects evaporated water in $L$ (≈ 2.5 %).

Merkel's driving force

The air's path: the operating linestep 4 of 4

From step 2 · water and air sides$dQ=L\,c_p\,dT \qquad dQ=G\,dh_a$
$G\,dh_a = L\,c_p\,dT$heat lost by water = heat gained by air
$h_a = h_{in}+\dfrac{L\,c_p}{G}\,(T-T_2)$integrate from the bottom, where air enters

$h_{in}$ = enthalpy of the entering air, fixed almost entirely by the wet bulb.

Slope $L\,c_p/G$: more water per kg of air makes the line steeper.

Interactive — drag the line

The gap between the curves is the driving force

Merkel number $KaV/L$smallest gap

A colder target or a higher $L/G$ closes the gap; the fill needed grows without limit as the line touches the curve.

What the operator reads

Range belongs to the users, approach to the tower

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Range}&=T_1-T_2=\frac{Q}{L\,c_p}\\ \text{Approach}&=T_2-T_{wb}\end{aligned}$$

$Q$ = heat duty picked up in the users, kW.

Range: set by the users' load and the circulation.

Approach: set by fill, fans, water per cell and weather.

The water balance

Evaporation leaves the salts behindstep 1 of 2

$$\begin{aligned}M&=E+D+B\\ N&=\frac{C_{circ}}{C_{mu}}=\frac{M}{B+D}\\ E&\approx 0.85\,Q/\lambda\end{aligned}$$

$C$ = conductivity (AIC-202), a measure of dissolved salts.

Interactive — choose the cycles

What cycles of concentration cost and savestep 2 of 2

From step 1$M=E+D+B \qquad N=\dfrac{M}{B+D}$
blowdown $B$make-up $M$conductivity

Past about 5 cycles make-up barely falls while the salts keep climbing: the saving flattens, the scaling risk does not.

Part 1 · summary

What Part 1 settled

  • About 85 % of the heat leaves by evaporation; the wet bulb is the limit.
  • Merkel: transfer is driven by $h_s-h_a$; $KaV/L$ measures the fill needed.
  • Range belongs to the users, approach to the tower and the weather.
  • Make-up replaces evaporation, drift and blowdown; blowdown sets the cycles.

Part 2 · Designing the unit

How is a cooling tower sized for a duty and a climate?

Part 2 · the plan

From a duty to equipment

  1. The design basiswhat the users and the climate fix before any sizing starts
  2. Tower demandthe Merkel number this duty requires
  3. Tower characteristicwhat a fill can deliver, and where the two meet
  4. Cells, fans and pumpsturning $L/G$ and pressure drops into equipment
  5. Basin and water treatmentinventory, trip margins and the cycles to run at

The design basis

What was fixed before sizing

ItemDesignWhere it comes from
Heat duty $Q$6.62 MWusers' coolers at full load
Circulation340 m³/husers' flow demand
Hot / cold water49.2 / 32.3 °Crange 16.9 °C
Design wet / dry bulb27 / 33 °Cassumed hot-humid Thai site
Approach5.3 °Ctower choice
Make-up water250 µS/cm, 300 kPa gcity supply (assumed)

Legacy module values: flows, temperatures, pressures, valve openings. Weather and water quality are engineering assumptions.

The design basis

Two choices decide the tower's size

Design wet bulb

Exceeded only a few percent of hours; too low leaves the tower short on hot days.

Approach

Usually 3–6 °C; each degree less needs much more fill.

Range

Not a tower choice: users' duty ÷ circulation.

Tower demand

Evaluating the Merkel integral by handstep 1 of 2

Part 1 gave an integral. Design needs a number: four points are enough.

Merkel integral · Part 1$\dfrac{KaV}{L}=\displaystyle\int_{T_2}^{T_1}\frac{c_p\,dT}{h_s-h_a}$
$$\frac{KaV}{L}\approx\frac{c_p\,(T_1-T_2)}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{4}\frac{1}{\Delta h_i}$$

$\Delta h_i=h_s-h_a$ at $T_2+0.1,\;0.4,\;0.6,\;0.9$ of the range (Chebyshev four-point rule).

Tower demand

The four points at designstep 2 of 2

$T$, °C$h_s$$h_a$$\Delta h$
34.2123.691.632.1
39.2159.3112.047.3
42.5188.3125.762.7
47.5242.0146.195.9
From step 1$\dfrac{KaV}{L}\approx\dfrac{c_p(T_1-T_2)}{4}\sum\dfrac{1}{\Delta h_i}$
$\dfrac{4.18\times16.7}{4}\times0.0788=1.37$design: 49.2 → 32.5 °C, $L/G$ = 0.98

Exact integral: 1.36. The coldest point carries most of it.

Tower characteristic

What a given fill can deliver

Demand says what the duty needs. Fill test data say what a tower gives.

$C$
fill constant from the vendor's test (here fitted to the design point)
–
$n$
slope of the fill curve, typically 0.5–0.8 (here 0.6)
–
$$\left(\frac{KaV}{L}\right)_{tower}=C\left(\frac{L}{G}\right)^{-n}\qquad C=1.34$$

More air per kg of water (lower $L/G$) gives more transfer per kg of water.

Interactive — size the air flow

The design point is where demand meets the fill

$L/G$ at the crossingair per cell (113 m³/h)fan power per cell

Cutting the approach from 5.5 to 3 °C needs about four times the fan power: a tight approach is bought with air.

Cells, fans and pumps

Why three cells instead of one big one

  • A cell can be taken out for cold weather or repair.
  • A failed fan costs a third of the air, not all of it.
  • Each cell: 113 m³/h of water, 32 kg/s of air, one 30 kW fan.

Cells, fans and pumps

Where the pump pressure goes

  • Three of four pumps run, 119 m³/h each; the fourth is the installed spare.
  • PI-201 = 98 kPa lift to the deck + spray-nozzle loss.
  • FCV-201 at 71 % leaves room to raise the flow to about 373 m³/h.

Basin and water treatment

The basin is the loop's reserve

area × level span90 m² × 2.0 m volume at 90 %162 m³ residence time at 358 m³/h27 min 1 % of level1.8 m³ LSL-201 pump start permissive15 % LSLL-201 pump trip8 %

The volume above 8 % is what buys time when the make-up fails; the pumps must stop before they lose suction.

Interactive — lose the make-up

How long before the pumps trip?

time to LSL-201 (15 %)time to LSLL-201 trip (8 %)

Losing all 11 m³/h of make-up leaves about 13 h: the basin buys time to act, not a fix.

Basin and water treatment

Design choices for the water itself

4 cycles

1000 µS/cm against 250 µS/cm city water; blowdown 2.7 m³/h.

pH 8.0–8.5

Acid (P-201) against scale, caustic (HS-205) against corrosion.

Biology

Chlorine P-220 (about 0.5 mg/L free) and a biocide P-221.

Filtration

Side-stream filter S-281 takes 15 m³/h, about 4 % of the flow.

Part 2 · summary

What Part 2 settled

  • Duty, circulation and design wet bulb are fixed first; range follows.
  • Demand $KaV/L$ = 1.36 at design; the fill characteristic meets it at $L/G$ ≈ 0.98.
  • A tighter approach costs fan power steeply.
  • Three cells, 3 + 1 pumps and a 162 m³ basin give turndown, spares and time.

Part 3 · Operating the unit

How does the operator keep the water cold enough, not too cold, and clean?

Part 3 · the plan

Five things an operator manages

  1. The handleswhat can be moved, and what each one moves
  2. Temperature follows the weatherfans and whole cells are the only trim
  3. Chemistry and inventorypH, cycles and level without over-correcting
  4. Health checksreading the approach and walking the cells
  5. Start-up and shutdown orderwhy each step comes where it does

The handles

What you want, and what you move

Design fixed the equipment. Operating is choosing which handle to move, and when.

To change……moveHow often
supply temperature TI-202fans on/off; whole cells in/outweather changes
circulation FIC-201set point; spare pump P-218load changes
basin level LIC-201nothing — AUTO on make-upwatch only
cycles AIC-202set point on blowdown FV-222rarely
pH AI-201acid P-201, caustic HS-205after a lab check
biology, filterP-220, P-221; backwash S-281routine

Temperature follows the weather

No controller holds TI-202

  • All fans on, design flow: each °C of wet bulb moves the cold water about 0.6 °C.
  • On a cool night the water drops below the band; on a hot day it rises above it.
  • The only trim: fewer fans, fewer cells.

Interactive — run the cells

Fans off, riser open: the wrong way to cool less

Fan (F) and riser (R) of each cell:

supply TI-202fan power

A cell with its fan stopped but water still on passes water almost as hot as it arrived: take whole cells out.

Temperature follows the weather

Three rules for trimming temperature

Whole cells

Stop the fan and close its riser together.

No starved cells

A running fan needs over 68 m³/h on its cell, or the E-20x LOAD (cell-load) alarm sounds.

Bypass last

Open HS-204 only when the fans are already off.

Health checks

Is it the weather or the tower?

What you seeApproach TI-202 − TI-231Hand thermometer at cells
weather hottersame or smallerall cells equal
fan stoppedlargerone cell near 45 °C
fill fouledlarger, slowlyone cell a few °C warm, fill slimy
users overloadedabout the sameall equal; TI-201 high

Trend the approach, not TI-202 alone: TI-202 moves with the weather every day.

Chemistry and inventory

Why pH doses are minutes, not seconds

$E$
alkalinity excess of the basin water (0 at pH 8.25)
meq/L
$\dot d$
dosing rate of caustic (+) or acid (−), 0.4 per minute
meq/L·min
$$\mathrm{pH}=8.25+3.2\,\tanh\!\left[0.33\,\operatorname{asinh}\!\left(\frac{E}{0.4}\right)\right]$$

The simulator's buffer curve: steep near 8.25, flat far from it.

Interactive — dose the basin

Same dose, very different effect

Buffer curve · previous slide$\mathrm{pH}=8.25+3.2\tanh[0.33\,\mathrm{asinh}(E/0.4)]$
pH after mixing

From pH 6.5 a 15-second dose barely registers; near 8.25 the same dose moves pH a lot, so dose, wait, then read.

Chemistry and inventory

Level and cycles run themselves — until the water runs short

LIC-201 in AUTO

Holds 90 % on city water; LCV-201 fails open.

AIC-202 in AUTO

Opens blowdown as salts rise; slow on purpose.

Make-up short

Check the city-water gauge; close blowdown (saves 2.7 m³/h).

Level too high

The basin overflows to drain: water and chemicals lost.

Health checks

What to check on every round

  • Hand thermometer under each cell; fans, plumes, vibration VI-212…214.
  • Pump gauges, casing temperature and noise.
  • Filter ΔP PDI-201: backwash near 35 kPa.
  • Acid, chlorine and biocide tanks; city-water gauge.
  • Laboratory sample: pH, conductivity, free chlorine.

Start-up and shutdown

Start-up: water first, air second, chemistry third

Fill basin ≥ 20 %→P-215 on bypass HS-204→Flow via FCV-201→Cells in, bypass shut →P-216, P-217; FIC-201 AUTO 340→Fans→Filter→Acid tank, pH→Chlorine, biocide, AIC-202→Users on

Pumps need suction (≥ 15 %) and a return path; fans need water on their cells.

Start-up and shutdown

Shutdown: the reverse, one cell at a time

Users off→Chlorine, biocide off→Filter off, P-217 off→Cell 3 out→Make-up closed →P-216 off, cell 2 out→FCV-201 closed→P-215 off, cell 1 out, bypass open

Match FIC-201 to the pumps still running, and never leave a pump against a closed valve.

Part 3 · summary

What Part 3 settled

  • TI-202 follows the weather; trim it with whole cells, never a fan alone.
  • Watch the approach and the hand thermometer to tell weather from faults.
  • pH responds slowly and nonlinearly: dose, wait, read, repeat.
  • Start-up builds water, then air, then chemistry; shutdown reverses it.

The loop at a glance

Block flow diagram of the circuit

Parts 1–3 treated the tower alone. Now follow the water through every unit.

Numbered circles are streams. Orange = warm return, blue = cold water, cyan = city water, grey = air, brown = chemicals, olive = filter purge.

Interactive — click a stream or a unit

Every stream at design

Click a number or a unit

Flows, temperatures and pressures are the simulator's design values.

The same 340 m³/h passes every point of the main loop; only 11 m³/h — the make-up — enters it.

Return, distribution and cooling

From the users to the top of the cells

  • Stream 1. Warm water returns at 49.2 °C; FCV-201 holds 340 m³/h for all users together.
  • Stream 2. The riser header lifts it about 10 m; PI-201 reads 172.5 kPa g.
  • Risers HS-201/202/203 put 113 m³/h on each cell; HS-204 can bypass to the basin.

Return, distribution and cooling

Inside a cell

Water, streams 2 → 7

Falls through the fill from 49.2 to 32.5 °C.

Air, streams 4 → 5

32 kg/s per cell enters at 33 °C, leaves saturated near 38 °C with 2.8 m³/h of vapour.

Drift, stream 6

About 0.07 m³/h of droplets escape the eliminators.

Basin, make-up and supply

Where the losses are replaced and the pressure made

  • Stream 8. City water through LCV-201 replaces about 11.2 m³/h.
  • Stream 9. Three pumps draw 358 m³/h from the pump pit.
  • Stream 10. 340 m³/h leaves at 32.3 °C and 345 kPa g; the users warm it back to 49.2 °C.

Side streams and protection

Small streams with big jobs

Filter, stream 11

15 m³/h through S-281, back to the basin.

Blowdown, stream 12

2.7 m³/h to drain through FV-222 holds 4 cycles.

Backwash and leak, 13–14

Zero unless backwashing or a tube leaks.

Protection

LSLL-201 stops the pumps before the basin runs dry; VSHH trips a vibrating fan.

Balances at design

Heat in equals heat out

$$Q_{users}=\sum Q_{cells}+Q_{mu}+Q_{basin}$$

MW at design; the sum closes to 0.00. $Q_{mu}$ = warming the city make-up.

Balances at design

Water and salts close too

Water, m³/hDesign
make-up FI-206+11.20
evaporation−8.40
drift−0.07
blowdown FI-222−2.71
sum0.02
Salts, µS/cm × m³/h ÷ 1000Design
in with make-up+2.80
out with blowdown−2.71
out with drift−0.07
sum0.02

A sum that drifts away from zero is the first sign of a loss you are not measuring.

Interactive — load the users

What the users' duty does to the loop

Part 1$\text{Range}=\dfrac{Q}{L\,c_p}\qquad E\approx 0.85\,Q/\lambda$
rangereturn TI-201 (supply 32.3 °C)evaporationmake-up at 4 cycles

Part 4 · summary

What Part 4 settled

  • 340 m³/h circulates; only 11 m³/h of city water enters.
  • Return 49.2 °C → cells → 32.5 °C → basin → supply 32.3 °C at 345 kPa g.
  • Side streams — filter, blowdown — keep the water usable.
  • Heat, water and salts each balance to zero at design.

Reading the P&ID

P&ID of the cooling water circuit

The flow sheet said what happens. The P&ID says how it is measured and moved.

Reading the P&ID

What the tag letters say

LetterFirst letter: measured variableLater letters: function
F · L · T · Pflow · level · temperature · pressureI = indicate
A · Vanalysis (pH, conductivity) · vibrationC = control
PDpressure difference (filter)V = valve, CV = control valve

ISA 5.1 convention: FIC-201 = flow indicating controller, loop 201; LSLL-201 = level switch low-low.

Three control loops

Each loop measures one thing and moves one valve

LoopMeasuresMovesFailsActionGain / reset
FIC-201return flowFCV-201openreverse0.3 / 5 s
LIC-201basin levelLCV-201 make-upopenreverse5 / 600 s
AIC-202conductivityFV-222 blowdowncloseddirect2 / 7200 s

Reverse: output up when PV falls. Direct: output up when PV rises (salts → blowdown).

Tuning a loop

What gain and reset do

$OP$
controller output to the valve
%
$e$
error: set point − measurement, in % of span
%
$K_c$
gain: output change per % of error
–
$T_i$
reset time: how fast the integral repeats the gain action
s
$$OP=OP_0+K_c\left(e+\frac{1}{T_i}\int e\,dt\right)$$

$OP_0$ = output when the loop was switched to AUTO — the bumpless start.

Interactive — tune the level loop

A basin is an integrator: give it gain, not a fast reset

PI law · previous slide$OP=OP_0+K_c\left(e+\tfrac{1}{T_i}\int e\,dt\right)$

At 20 min the losses jump from 11.2 to 16.8 m³/h (damaged drift eliminators).

lowest levelovershoot above 90 %LCV-201 at 4 h

Low gain with a short reset lets the level dip and overshoot for hours; the design tuning (5 / 600 s) holds it within 0.8 %.

Fail-safe positions

Where the valves go when the air is lost

FCV-201 opens

The users keep their cooling water.

LCV-201 opens

The basin keeps its water; overflow beats dry pumps.

FV-222 closes

No water wasted while blowdown is uncontrolled.

Each fail position protects what matters most: cooling first, inventory second, water cost third.

Interactive — trip it

Cause and effect: what each event does

Only LSLL-201 and the ESD stop the pumps; a fan trip stops one fan, and air failure trips nothing — valves just go to their safe side.

The five DCS displays

Water and chemistry: the balance by difference

  • Make-up = evaporation + blowdown + the rest; the rest should be near zero.
  • Cycles, pH, acid tank, dosing pumps, filter state.
  • A growing "rest" means drift, a leak or overflow.

Part 7 · Other unit operations in the loop

What do the pumps, the users' exchanger, the filter and the dosing each add?

The equipment around the tower

  1. Circulating pumps in parallelwhere the flow and header pressure come from
  2. The users' exchangerwhy flow and fouling set the process temperature

Circulating pumps

Pumps in parallel share the flowstep 1 of 2

The tower cools the water; the pumps must first deliver it — against which pressures?

$\Delta P$
pressure the pumps add (discharge − suction)
kPa
$H_0$

kPa
$Q$

m³/h
$n$

–
$a$

kPa/(m³/h)²
$$\Delta P = H_0 - a\left(\frac{Q}{n}\right)^2$$

Below about 13 % basin level the pumps cavitate and the curve collapses.

Operating point = pump curve meets system curvestep 2 of 2

users' flow FI-202PI-202 / PI-201

A fourth pump at the same valve raises the pressure more than the flow; FIC-201 then closes FCV-201 to hold 340 m³/h.

The users' exchanger

One lumped cooler stands for all usersstep 1 of 2

$C_h,\;C_c$
heat-capacity rate of process (132.5) and cooling water (392 at 340 m³/h)
kW/K
$UA$
overall conductance: 257 at design, ∝ flow$^{0.8}$ × clean fraction
kW/K
$N,\;C_r$
$N=UA/C_{min}$ transfer units; $C_r=C_{min}/C_{max}$
–

–
$$\varepsilon=\frac{1-e^{-N(1-C_r)}}{1-C_r\,e^{-N(1-C_r)}}\qquad Q=\varepsilon\,C_{min}\,(95-T_{202})$$

Counter-current exchanger; the process enters at 95 °C.

Interactive — foul the users

What the users seestep 2 of 2

Step 1$Q=\varepsilon\,C_{min}\,(95-T_{202})$
users' outlet TI-203return TI-201duty

Fouling makes TI-203 rise while TI-201 falls: less heat reaches the water, so the tower looks fine.

Side-stream filter

Filter S-281 and its backwash

  1. Isolate: close HS-207, HS-208.
  2. Backwash: P-219, HS-208A, HS-209 about 3 min.
  3. Rinse: HS-210 open, HS-209 shut.
  4. Stop P-219, close purges, filter back on line.

The filter is a side stream: a plugged filter raises PDI-201 but does not cut the cooling.

Chemical dosing and biology

What each chemical does

$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{H_2SO_4}+\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}&\rightarrow\mathrm{CaSO_4}+2\,\mathrm{CO_2}+2\,\mathrm{H_2O}\\ \mathrm{Cl_2}+\mathrm{H_2O}&\rightarrow\mathrm{HOCl}+\mathrm{HCl}\end{aligned}$$

First: acid destroys the bicarbonate alkalinity that would scale as CaCO₃.

Second: hypochlorous acid HOCl kills bacteria and algae; it decays within hours.

Caustic (NaOH) raises pH when it falls; the biocide is a second, slower line of defence.

Part 7 · summary

What Part 7 settled

  • Parallel pumps meet the system curve; FIC-201 trims the valve to hold flow.
  • The users' temperature depends on flow, supply temperature and fouling.
  • The filter is a side stream; backwash in the right order.
  • Acid fights scale, caustic corrosion, chlorine and biocide biology.

What takes points off the score

Six graded procedures

Cold start-up and normal shutdown1 of 3

Cold start-up · limit 4 h

Objective: bring an empty, stopped circuit to design and hand it to the users.

Start: basin 10 %, motors off · 15 steps

Normal shutdown · limit 30 min

Objective: take the tower off line cell by cell with no pump deadheaded.

Start: users off · 9 steps

Grade /10: 0 if unsafe; −4 out of order, −2 over time, −1 users not told.

Six graded procedures

Power dip and filter backwash2 of 3

Power dip · limit 15 min

Objective: restore cooling water after every motor drops out.

Start: design; the dip arrives at 20 s · users without water over 2 min = unsafe

TS-B filter backwash · limit 30 min

Objective: clean a plugged filter in the correct valve order.

Start: design; plugging begins at 30 s · 6 tracked steps

Six graded procedures

Flow reduction and optimisation3 of 3

TS-C flow reduction · limit 40 min

Objective: cut circulation 10 % in 2 % steps and handle an unknown upset on the way.

Start: design · hold TI-202, flow and pH for 5 min at the end

Optimisation · 45 min, graded live

Objective: cut electricity to 105 kW or less on a cool evening.

Checked at the end: TI-202, TI-203, kW, no starved fan, no alarm

Training exercises

Twenty-one exercises, five skill areas

Each one starts at design; one upset arrives about 30 s after loading.

Pumps and flow · 6

Keep the users supplied when circulation changes.

Cells, fans, weather · 6

Hold TI-202 with whole cells; judge by the approach.

Water and inventory · 4

Close the water balance; protect the basin.

Chemistry and filter · 3

Keep pH and the filter in band.

Utilities · 2

Know fail positions; restart in order.

The name of the upset is not shown: find it from the DCS, the field and the laboratory.

Troubleshooting cases

Six stages for a problem with no name

Troubleshooting cases give only a situation: no fault name, no hint.

The order matters: decide safety first, then define, explore and test hypotheses before acting.

Troubleshooting cases

Temperature and water1 of 3

TE-1 Coolers running hot this afternoon

Decide whether the tower is at fault.

TE-2 Supply warm with every fan running

Find why the tower lost capacity.

TE-3 Level falling, LCV-201 wide open

Find the cause and protect the pumps.

TE-4 Make-up much higher than last week

Account for every cubic metre of make-up.

Troubleshooting cases

Instruments and equipment2 of 3

TE-5 Supply and return do not agree

Decide which reading to believe, and why.

TE-6 Users too warm, TI-202 looks fine

Resolve a complaint that the DCS contradicts.

TE-7 Filter ΔP climbing

Confirm the cause and restore the filter.

TE-8 pH keeps drifting up

Bring the pH back into band and keep it there.

Troubleshooting cases

Users, fans, weather and biology3 of 3

TE-9 Users hot but our water is cold

Locate the problem: inside or outside the tower.

TE-10 Cell E-203 fan tripped again

Decide whether a repeated trip may be reset.

TE-11 Cold supply water this morning

Bring the supply back into band safely.

TE-12 Free chlorine zero on the lab report

Restore the free chlorine and explain the cause.

Short drills

Four drills that need no fault

What-if (6 events × 8 tags)

Predict which way each tag moves 30 min after an event.

Trend matching (4 of 6 events)

Name the event from its 10-minute trend.

Scrambles (3)

Put start-up, shutdown and backwash steps in order.

DCS reading sheet (14 tags)

Read values and alarm limits correctly.

Part 8 · summary

What Part 8 settled

  • Every exercise: load, read, diagnose, act, tell, debrief.
  • Procedures are graded on safety, order and time.
  • Training and troubleshooting both hide the upset: find it from the evidence.
  • Drills build prediction and reading skills between exercises.

Key Takeaways

Key Takeaways

1

Judge the tower by its approach to the wet bulb, not by TI-202 alone.

2

Trim temperature with whole cells: fan off and riser closed together.

3

Close the water balance to find losses no meter shows.

4

Dose chemicals, wait, then read — and check the lab before trusting a probe.

5

Restore circulation first: the users cannot wait for anything else.
